title: Arrays & Data Collections
description: Learn how to store, organise, and manage multiple values using arrays and basic collections in C#. Master arrays, lists, and collection methods to build scalable applications and prepare for game development.
completionText: You are ready for Module 8, where object-oriented programming teaches you how to create custom classes and objects for building professional applications and games.

lessons.title: Introduction to Arrays
objectives: Explain what arrays are and why they matter.
Identify problems with creating separate variables.
Describe array indexing and zero-based positioning.
theory: An array is a collection of values all of the same type stored in a single variable. Without arrays, storing ten scores would require ten separate variables: score1, score2, ..., score10. This is tedious and hard to manage.
With an array, you store all ten scores in one variable: int[] scores = new int[10]; Each score has a position in the array.
C# uses zero-based indexing. The first element is at index 0, the second at index 1, and so on. An array of 10 elements has indices 0 through 9. This is universal across programming languages.

Arrays are especially useful when processing groups of related data. Game inventories, enemy lists, high scores, and player statistics all use arrays. Professional programs rely on arrays and collections.
Arrays are fixed size. Once you declare int[] scores = new int[10];, the array always holds 10 elements. If you need a flexible size, you can use a List instead, which you will learn in Lesson 6.
terms: A collection of values of the same type.
The position of an element in an array.
lessons.tryIt: Create an array of five numbers and print each one using its index.
lessons.challenge: Create an array of animal names and print them all using a loop.
mistakes: Remember arrays are zero-indexed.
Arrays are fixed size once created.
All elements must be the same type.
Index errors cause exceptions.
lessons.summary: Arrays store multiple values of the same type in one variable. Zero-based indexing positions elements. Arrays are essential for managing groups of data.
quiz: A collection of values of same type
Array size is fixed at creation.
All array elements must be the same type.

lessons.title: Creating and Initialising Arrays
objectives: Declare arrays with the correct syntax.
Understand array size and default values.
Create arrays for different data types.
theory: An array declaration specifies the type and size. int[] scores = new int[5]; creates an integer array with 5 elements. The new keyword allocates memory.
When declared this way, elements receive default values. Numeric arrays default to 0. Boolean arrays default to false. String arrays default to null.
You can also initialise an array with specific values. int[] scores = {90, 85, 88}; creates an array and fills it immediately. The size is inferred from the number of values.
Arrays can hold any data type. string[] names holds text. bool[] flags holds true/false values. double[] temperatures holds decimal numbers. char[] letters holds individual characters.
Choosing between empty initialization and value initialization depends on your needs. Empty arrays are useful when filling data later. Value initialization is useful when you know the data upfront.
lessons.tryIt: Create an array of five player scores, then change the first score to a new value.
lessons.challenge: Create three arrays: one of strings, one of integers, and one of booleans. Print all values.
mistakes: Use the correct type syntax (int[], string[], etc.).
Remember the new keyword for empty arrays.
Array size is fixed after creation.
All values must match the array type.
lessons.summary: Arrays are declared with type and size. Initialise with defaults or specific values. Different types create different arrays. Modify elements using index assignment.
quiz: Type and square brackets precede the name.

lessons.title: Accessing and Modifying Array Values
objectives: Read values from arrays using indexes.
theory: Reading an array element uses the index. int firstScore = scores[0]; reads the first element. Console.WriteLine(weapons[2]); prints the third element.
Changing an array element uses assignment. scores[0] = 95; replaces the first element with 95. inventory[2] = "Key"; changes the third inventory item.
Index boundaries are critical. An array of size 5 has valid indices 0 through 4. Accessing scores[5] is out of bounds and causes an IndexOutOfRangeException.
The .Length property tells you the array size. scores.Length returns 5 for an array of 5 elements. Use it to prevent index errors: if (i < scores.Length)
Common mistakes include forgetting zero-based indexing, accessing beyond array bounds, and confusing index numbers. Always verify indices are within 0 to length−1.
lessons.tryIt: Create an array, modify a value, and print it before and after the change.
lessons.challenge: Create an array and verify the index is valid before accessing each element.
mistakes: Remember zero-based indexing starts at 0.
Use .Length to check valid range.
Index out of bounds causes exceptions.
Always verify before accessing unfamiliar indices.
lessons.summary: Access array elements using indexes within bounds. Modify with assignment. Use .Length to check validity. Index errors are a common source of bugs.
quiz: This exception is thrown for invalid indices.
Length is a property without parentheses.

lessons.title: Looping Through Arrays
theory: Processing every array element is common. A for loop with a counter is perfect for this. for (int i = 0; i < scores.Length; i++) { } iterates through each index.
The foreach loop is even simpler when you only need the values, not indices. foreach (int score in scores) { } automatically provides each element.
For loops give you the index, useful when you need to know position or modify elements. Foreach is cleaner when you just want to read each value.
Nested loops process multi-dimensional data. Outer loops iterate rows, inner loops iterate columns. This is essential for game grids and matrices.
Combining loops and arrays unlocks powerful data processing. Calculating sums, finding averages, searching for values, and transforming data all use loops over arrays.
lessons.tryIt: Create an array and calculate the sum using a for loop.
lessons.challenge: Use a foreach loop to find the average of array values.
mistakes: For loop condition uses < not <=.
Use scores[i], not scores.
Foreach creates a new variable each iteration.
Initialize accumulator variables before loops.
lessons.summary: For loops process arrays by index. Foreach loops process by value. Choose based on needs: for when you need index, foreach when you don't. Both are essential.
quiz: Foreach is for reading without index.

lessons.title: Multi-Dimensional Arrays
objectives: Apply to game maps and grids.
theory: A multi-dimensional array has rows and columns. A 2D array is like a table. int[,] grid = new int[3, 3]; creates a 3×3 grid.
Access 2D elements with two indices. grid[0, 1] accesses row 0, column 1. grid[2, 2] is bottom-right of a 3×3 grid.
Looping through 2D arrays requires nested loops. Outer loop iterates rows, inner loop iterates columns. for (int row = 0; row < 3; row++) { for (int col = 0; col < 3; col++) { } }
Games use 2D arrays for maps, tile systems, and game boards. A chess board is 8×8. A tic-tac-toe board is 3×3. Dungeon levels are large grids.
Higher dimensions exist: 3D arrays, 4D arrays, etc. But 2D is most common and sufficient for most applications. 3D arrays are rare in basic programming.
terms: Two indices for row and column.
lessons.tryIt: Create a 2×2 grid, set all values, and print them using nested loops.
lessons.challenge: Create a tic-tac-toe board and print it with X and O symbols.
mistakes: Use comma between dimensions, not separate brackets.
Nested loops: outer for rows, inner for columns.
Two indices required for 2D access.
Check both dimensions for bounds.
lessons.summary: Multi-dimensional arrays store tabular data. 2D arrays use row and column indices. Nested loops process grids. Games use 2D arrays for maps and boards.
quiz: Outer loop rows, inner loop columns.

lessons.title: Lists (List<T>)
theory: An array has fixed size. A List grows and shrinks dynamically. List<string> inventory = new List<string>(); creates an empty list.
Lists use angle brackets <> to specify the item type. List<int> holds integers. List<string> holds text. The syntax reads 'List of type'.
Add items with Add(). inventory.Add("Sword"); adds a sword. Remove items with Remove() or RemoveAt().
Lists have many useful methods. Count returns the number of items. Contains() checks if an item exists. Clear() removes all items.
Use arrays for fixed-size data. Use Lists for dynamic data. Game inventories, enemy lists, and collectible items all benefit from Lists because they change during gameplay.
lessons.tryIt: Create a list of numbers, add five values, print them all, then remove one.
lessons.challenge: Create a list of player names and remove anyone whose name starts with 'Z'.
mistakes: Use angle brackets for type: List<type>.
Count is a property, not a method.
Lists use the same index access as arrays.
RemoveAt uses index; Remove uses value.
lessons.summary: Lists are dynamic arrays that grow and shrink. Use Add to insert, Remove to delete, Count to check size. Lists are essential for data that changes during runtime.
quiz: Both methods are valid for different purposes.

lessons.title: Useful Collection Methods
theory: Lists have many useful methods beyond Add and Remove. Add() appends to the end. RemoveAt(int index) removes by position. Remove(T item) removes by value.
Contains(T item) returns true if the item exists, useful for inventory checks. IndexOf(T item) returns the position of an item, or −1 if not found.
Clear() removes all items. Count returns the number of items. Insert(int index, T item) adds an item at a specific position.
Practical examples show method power. Inventory systems check Contains before using an item. Quest systems clear objectives with Clear(). Undo systems use RemoveAt on the most recent action.

Mastering these methods makes programs cleaner and more efficient. Instead of manual loops searching for items, Contains does it directly. Professional code uses built-in methods rather than reinventing them.
lessons.tryIt: Create a list, use Contains to check for an item, then use IndexOf to find its position.
lessons.challenge: Build an inventory where you can add, remove, and search for weapons by name.
mistakes: IndexOf returns −1 if not found, not null.
Insert shifts other items, does not replace.
Remove removes first occurrence only.
Clear removes everything permanently in that session.
lessons.summary: Essential List methods include Add, Remove, Contains, IndexOf, Insert, and Clear. These methods handle common tasks efficiently. Master them for professional code.
quiz: Remove uses value, RemoveAt uses index
Remove takes item, RemoveAt takes index.

lessons.title: Practice Project · Inventory Management System
objectives: Build a complete RPG inventory system.
theory: This project brings together all Module 7 concepts. You will create a simple RPG-style inventory system where players can view, add, and remove items.
The program uses a List to store inventory items. A menu offers choices: view inventory, add item, remove item, search for item, or exit.
For each choice, appropriate methods handle the logic. View loops through items. Add uses Add(). Remove uses RemoveAt after finding the index. Search uses IndexOf.
Input validation ensures menu choices are valid and item names are not empty. Error handling manages invalid operations gracefully.
A complete system demonstrates professional software design: clear menus, input validation, appropriate data structures, and logical method organization.
lessons.tryIt: Build a basic version where you can add and view items.
lessons.challenge: Extend the system to show item count, limit inventory size, or track item quantities.
mistakes: Validate all user input before using it.
Check if inventory is empty before viewing.
Use appropriate List methods for each operation.
Handle edge cases like empty names.
lessons.summary: A complete inventory system demonstrates practical list usage. Menu-driven interfaces, input validation, and appropriate methods create professional applications.
quiz: Remove takes the item name directly.
